strengths: Addresses a genuine and important practical gap: unsupervised model selection/misspecification diagnosis in Bayesian imaging where no ground truth or replicate measurements are available, and where priors are large black-box ML models (diffusion, PnP) that are incompatible with classical marginal-likelihood techniques.

The core methodological idea—combining data fission (measurement splitting by noise injection) with Bayesian cross-validation/partial predictive summaries—is a reasonably novel and elegant way to sidestep the single-measurement constraint intrinsic to imaging applications.

Solid theoretical grounding: the paper carefully relates its proposed summaries to posterior predictive checks and the marginal likelihood as limiting cases (α→0), and derives closed-form expressions in a tractable Gaussian toy model to validate intuition about bias/variance trade-offs controlled by α.

Reasonably broad and varied experimental validation: kernel/likelihood selection on natural images, OOD/prior misspecification detection for diffusion priors on natural images and MRI (brain vs. knee), with both mild and strong misspecification scenarios, and additional Poisson-noise experiments in the supplement.
Clear improvement over an existing lightweight baseline (Bayesian/empirical Bayesian residuals), with large margins in kernel selection accuracy (86.7%/100% vs 40–60%).

Good practical properties: compatible with any posterior sampler (Langevin PnP, diffusion guidance), computationally lightweight relative to nested sampling or harmonic mean estimators, and empirically shown to need relatively few MC samples for reliable use despite theoretically slow asymptotic convergence.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: code repository referenced, extensive implementation details and hyperparameters reported in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: The method's practical reliability is quite sensitive to the choice of hyperparameter α and to the embedding/scoring rule (LPIPS vs. likelihood vs. Dinov2), and the paper offers no principled/automatic procedure for selecting these — Fig. 15 and the MRI ablation (Dinov2 raising accuracy from ~86% to 100%) show the results can shift substantially with these choices, effectively requiring case-by-case tuning that undermines the claimed generality.

Statistical evaluation is based on fairly small test sets (60–90 natural images, 50 MRI scans per class), so the reported Type I error/power percentages have considerable sampling uncertainty; no confidence intervals or repeated-trial variance are reported.

No direct empirical comparison against existing OOD-detection baselines from the literature (e.g., diffusion-based unsupervised OOD detectors such as [48] or [31]) in the main OOD experiments, despite these being discussed in the related work; only the likelihood model-selection experiment is benchmarked against a prior method.

The theoretical analysis with exact/asymptotic guarantees (bias reduction via K, convergence behavior) is confined to a simple linear-Gaussian toy model; no formal statistical guarantees (e.g., consistency or error bounds) are provided for the general nonlinear/deep-prior setting used in the main experiments, leaving the practical estimator's accuracy essentially empirical.

The method implicitly assumes the noise model itself is correctly specified (since data fission relies on exact knowledge of the noise distribution for the splitting operation); misspecification of the noise model is not addressed, which could be an important failure mode in real imaging pipelines.

Mixed results in the MRI experiment (Φ1 sometimes outperforming Φ2 or vice versa depending on organ/acceleration) suggest inconsistent reliability of the posterior-based rule across modalities without further tuning, which the paper acknowledges but does not resolve.

Model selection accuracy in the kernel experiment, while much better than baselines, is not perfect in the single-shot regime (86.7%) even though the candidate kernels were deliberately designed to be very close to one another; it remains unclear how performance degrades with a larger number of candidate models or subtler differences.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: unsupervised model selection and misspecification diagnosis for Bayesian imaging models using only a single noisy measurement, which is the realistic setting in most imaging applications.

The core methodological idea—combining Bayesian cross-validation with data fission/measurement splitting—is a novel and elegant way to circumvent the lack of replicate measurements, and the authors clearly connect it to the marginal likelihood in a limiting case (alpha to 0), giving the approach a principled theoretical anchor.

The method is explicitly designed to be agnostic to the sampler and prior, and the paper demonstrates this by successfully integrating it with quite different Bayesian imaging pipelines (PnP Langevin/SK-ROCK and DiffPIR diffusion posterior sampling), which is a meaningful practical contribution.

Two complementary scoring rules are proposed (likelihood-based and posterior/perceptual-based) that are well-motivated by the failure modes of each (e.g., insensitivity of the likelihood rule to null-space information in rank-deficient problems), and both are validated empirically.

The experimental evaluation is fairly extensive: a controlled Gaussian toy analysis validating the theory and bias/variance trade-offs, blur-kernel selection experiments with comparison to an existing baseline (Bayesian/empirical Bayesian residuals) showing clear accuracy gains, and OOD/misspecification detection experiments on natural images and MRI with reasonable Type I error and power statistics.

Supplementary material contains substantial additional analysis (numerical convergence behavior, sensitivity to alpha, embedding choice, Poisson noise extension, MRI single-shot results) that strengthens confidence in robustness of the claims.
Code is stated to be publicly available, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Formal statistical guarantees are largely limited to the toy Gaussian model; for the realistic deep-prior experiments the approach is validated only empirically, and no theoretical results characterize bias, consistency, or calibration of the proposed test statistics under general (non-Gaussian, deep prior) models.

The Type I error control demonstrated in experiments relies on empirically estimating a 95th percentile threshold from a reference in-distribution dataset; this makes the procedure not purely 'single-measurement unsupervised' in the strictest sense, since it still requires a representative reference dataset for calibration, which is a real practical dependency not fully discussed as a limitation in the main text.

The posterior-based/perceptual scoring rule depends on the choice of embedding (LPIPS, CLIP, Dinov2), and the supplementary material shows results can change noticeably with this choice (e.g., Dinov2 raising MRI accuracy to 100%); this sensitivity and the lack of clear guidance on embedding selection for new domains is a practical limitation not thoroughly addressed.

The Monte Carlo convergence analysis in the Gaussian case (SM Fig. 11) shows slow convergence, and while the authors argue empirically that few samples suffice for the imaging experiments, this claim is not rigorously justified and could be dataset- or task-dependent, raising concerns about generalization of the low sample counts (K, N) used.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat narrow: the kernel-selection experiment compares only against Bayesian/empirical Bayesian residual methods, and no comparison is made against nested sampling-based marginal likelihood estimators (mentioned in Background) even on smaller/simplified problems where they might be tractable, which would have better substantiated the accuracy-versus-cost trade-off claimed in the paper.

The choice of the splitting parameter alpha is shown to matter substantially for detection power (SM Fig. 15), yet no principled/automatic procedure for choosing alpha is proposed; practitioners are left to tune it manually, which could hinder reproducibility across new applications.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: unsupervised model selection and misspecification diagnosis for imaging inverse problems with modern, implicit (deep-learning-based) priors, where ground truth and repeated measurements are unavailable.

Clean theoretical grounding: the paper carefully relates the proposed cross-validation summaries to posterior predictive checks and proves (Proposition 1, with full proof in the appendix) that the method recovers the marginal likelihood in the limit alpha -> 0, giving a principled interpretation of the alpha parameter as a bias/variance/cost trade-off knob.

Method is sampler-agnostic and compatible with modern black-box imaging samplers (PnP Langevin, DiffPIR-type diffusion samplers), which is practically valuable given the diversity of priors used in the field.

Extensive and diverse experimental validation: toy Gaussian analysis with exact solutions, blur-kernel model selection with clear improvement over existing residual-based baselines (Vidal et al.), OOD detection on natural images and MRI with well-designed ID/moderate-OOD/strong-OOD splits and Type I error/power reporting, comparison against a nested-sampling evidence estimator, and several ablations (embedding choice, Poisson noise, sample-quality degradation, number of MC samples).

Good transparency about failure modes and limitations, e.g., degraded power at high blur/mild misspecification, sensitivity to embedding choice (CLIP fails while LPIPS/DINOv2/DreamSim work reasonably), and breakdown when the underlying sampler itself fails.
Code availability statement and detailed algorithmic/implementation appendix supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The perceptual/posterior-based scoring rule (Φ2) depends heavily on a chosen embedding space; the ablation shows large sensitivity (CLIP embeddings essentially fail), and no principled guidance is given for selecting embeddings for a new task beyond trial-and-error.

The splitting parameter alpha critically controls the accuracy/cost/discrimination trade-off, but the guidance for choosing it in practice is largely qualitative/empirical (based on toy Gaussian intuition and ad hoc tuning per experiment) rather than a principled selection rule for real, high-dimensional problems.

OOD/misspecification detection power decreases substantially in more realistic 'mild misspecification' or high-information-loss regimes (e.g., high blur, Met-Faces case), and the method can fail silently when the underlying posterior sampler itself is of poor quality (Section E.5), without a built-in diagnostic for this failure mode.

Despite claims of being computationally efficient relative to nested sampling, the method still requires K x N (x L) full posterior sampling runs per evaluated model, which is non-trivial for diffusion-based samplers (e.g., ~1800s per image for DiffPIR in Table 4); scalability to larger datasets or many candidate models is not deeply analyzed.

Threshold-based OOD testing relies on an empirically calibrated percentile from a reference ID dataset rather than a distribution-free or theoretically justified test statistic, so the reported Type I error control is empirical rather than guaranteed.

The paper positions itself against Shoushtari et al. (2025) as the only related unsupervised OOD method but does not provide a direct empirical comparison against it, despite testing on a similar MRI/diffusion setting, leaving the relative merits unclear.

The theoretical analysis is restricted to a linear-Gaussian toy model; error/bias characterizations of the MC estimators in realistic high-dimensional, nonlinear/non-Gaussian imaging settings remain largely empirical.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: unsupervised model selection and misspecification diagnosis in Bayesian imaging inverse problems using only a single noisy measurement, with no need for ground truth or paired data.

Novel and elegant combination of data fission (measurement splitting by noise injection) with Bayesian cross-validation, yielding a principled partial-predictive framework that is agnostic to the choice of prior/sampler and compatible with modern black-box priors such as diffusion and plug-and-play models.

Solid theoretical grounding: the toy Gaussian analysis (Sec. 4.1, App. C) gives clear intuition on the role of the splitting parameter α and the number of noise realizations K, and Proposition 1 rigorously shows the proposed posterior-predictive quantity converges to the marginal likelihood as α→0, connecting the method to the gold-standard Bayes factor.

Two complementary, well-motivated scoring rules (likelihood-based and embedding-based posterior rule) are proposed to probe different aspects of misspecification (likelihood vs. prior), which is a practically useful design choice illustrated concretely in the ill-posed MRI/deblurring settings.

Extensive and diverse experimental validation: kernel/likelihood selection for deblurring, OOD/prior misspecification detection on natural images (multiple test datasets spanning mild to strong OOD) and MRI reconstruction, plus ablations on embeddings, noise models (Poisson), sample-quality robustness, and a comparison against a nested-sampling evidence estimator (ProxNest) that corroborates the method's rankings.

Substantial accuracy gains over existing unsupervised baselines (Bayesian/empirical-Bayes residual methods), and favorable computational cost relative to marginal-likelihood estimation via nested sampling.

Good transparency in appendices regarding implementation details, sampler settings, and computational overhead (Table 4), supporting reproducibility, and the method is packaged as a general algorithm (Algorithm 1).
weaknesses: The OOD/misspecification testing procedure still requires a reference in-distribution dataset to calibrate the rejection threshold (95th percentile), which partially compromises the 'single measurement, fully unsupervised' framing emphasized in the abstract/introduction.

Selection of the key hyperparameter α is largely heuristic; while the Gaussian toy analysis offers intuition, no principled data-driven rule is given for real applications, and empirical results (Fig. 18) show non-trivial sensitivity of detection power/type-I error to this choice.

The method's diagnostic reliability is coupled to the quality of the underlying posterior sampler; Section E.5 shows that when the sampler itself degrades/breaks down (e.g., too few diffusion steps), the estimators fail without any independent signal of this failure mode, which is a practically important limitation not fully resolved.

Performance depends noticeably on the chosen embedding for the posterior-based rule (LPIPS/Dinov2 work well, CLIP fails, Dreamsim over-rejects ID data), and no general guidance is offered for selecting/adapting embeddings to new imaging modalities (acknowledged for MRI, where natural-image-trained perceptual metrics may be suboptimal).

Single-shot accuracy is imperfect in more challenging discrimination tasks (e.g., 86.7% for closely related blur kernels, and mildly OOD Met-Faces misclassified at high blur), indicating the method's resolving power degrades under weak identifiability or fine model differences.

Beyond empirical Type I error/power tables, there is limited theoretical analysis of the finite-sample statistical properties (bias/variance, asymptotic guarantees) of the proposed testing procedure for realistic (non-Gaussian, nonlinear) imaging models.
